Dozens of retired coal-fired power plants could find new life providing backup or emergency power for the electricity grid (电网) — except this time without the need for fossil fuels.

During the grid’s low-demand periods, these machines would change cheap electricity into heat, which would remain stored within the dirt at a temperature of about 600°C. During times of high power demand, the heat could be transferred out of the dirt via pipes of heated liquid.
Energy storage like this is necessary to supplement renewable power sources, such as wind and solar, which cannot provide energy continuously.
And dirt is cheaper, more abundant and more widely available than other types of long-term energy storage, such as lithium batteries or hydrogen fuel.
Most dirt includes naturally heat-resistant materials, such as silicon dioxide and aluminum oxide, says Austin Vernon at Standard Thermal in Oklahoma.
His start-up is looking to commercialize this “heat battery” technology for repowering retired coal power plants, especially at sites with nearby solar or wind power sources.
Retired coal plants will turn into heat batteries by 2030.
Repurposed coal plants can bring in economic benefits.
